input: Rule records against their source, part 1 (reading comfort). packages/kit/src/data/neuro.ts: neuro-line-length "A line of reading text holds at most 80 letters." source wcag('1.4.8 Visual Presentation (level AAA)'); neuro-line-height "Reading text has a line height of at least 1.5." sources 1.4.8 and wcag('1.4.12 Text Spacing'); neuro-no-justified-text "Reading text is aligned to one side, never stretched to both." source 1.4.8. Compared with the text at https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/ and with README: "**Stricter than the source.** Some rules ask for more than the standard they cite. The record's source line says so each time." and PROGRESS.md: "Where a rule asks for more than its source, the record says so."
observed: WCAG 2.2, 1.4.8: "For the visual presentation of blocks of text, a mechanism is available to achieve the following: ... Width is no more than 80 characters ... Text is not justified ... Line spacing (leading) is at least space-and-a-half within paragraphs" and "Note 1 Content is not required to use these values. The requirement is that a mechanism is available for users to change these presentation aspects." WCAG 2.2, 1.4.12: "no loss of content or functionality occurs by setting all of the following ... Line height (line spacing) to at least 1.5 times the font size" and "Note 1 Content is not required to use these text spacing values." The three records turn 'a mechanism is available' into a requirement on the page itself, which both criteria expressly do not ask, and none of the three source lines says the kit asks for more. 1.4.12 does not support neuro-line-height at all (it is the source of neuro-text-spacing).

input: Rule records against their source, part 3: records that ask for more than the cited criterion with no word about it in the source line. (a) neuro-motion-can-stop: "Anything that moves for more than five seconds has a visible control that pauses it." source '2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide'. (b) behavior-target-size: "Everything that can be tapped is at least 24 by 24 pixels." source '2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum)'. (c) neuro-error-recovery: "...and keeps what the person typed." sources 3.3.1, 3.3.3. (d) neuro-no-surprise: "Nothing opens, moves, or changes page until the person asks for it." sources '3.2.1 On Focus', '3.2.2 On Input'. (e) behavior-dialog-keys: "A window over the page takes the keyboard focus, keeps it inside..." source APG 'Dialog (Modal) Pattern', against the walk in packages/kit/src/data/walks.ts.
observed: (a) 2.2.2: "...(1) starts automatically, (2) lasts more than five seconds, and (3) is presented in parallel with other content, there is a mechanism for the user to pause, stop, or hide it unless the movement ... is part of an activity where it is essential": the source accepts stop or hide, does not ask for a visible control, and has two conditions and an exception the record omits. (b) 2.5.8 lists five exceptions (Spacing, Equivalent, Inline, User Agent Control, Essential); the record says 'everything'; the check applies only the Inline one. (c) 3.3.1: "the item that is in error is identified and the error is described to the user in text"; 3.3.3: suggestions "if ... known"; neither says input is kept. (d) 3.2.1 and 3.2.2 are about a change of context caused by focus or by changing a setting, not about a page that changes with no action. (e) APG: "Tab: Moves focus to the next tabbable element inside the dialog. If focus is on the last tabbable element inside the dialog, moves focus to the first"; the kit's walk accepts the focus on document.body after Tab (step 'expect-focus-not-behind'), so here the kit asks for less than its source and less than its own record ('keeps it inside'). None of these five source lines says the record differs from the source, against README "The record's source line says so each time." Sources that did match: 1.4.2 (with its note), 1.4.10, 2.3.1, 2.3.3 (AAA, noted), 2.4.13 (AAA, noted), 3.3.2 (noted), 3.3.4 (noted), 4.1.2, 4.1.3, 1.1.1, COGA Objectives 1, 4, 5 and pattern 4.5.6 'Use Clear Visible Labels', APG Tabs ('Home (Optional)', 'End (Optional)').

input: The usage example of packages/kit/README.md ('How to use it'), run as written against packages/kit/fixtures/good.html: `for (const fn of Object.keys(checks)) findings.push(...await page.evaluate(`(${checks[fn]})(document)`));`
observed: 'README loop threw after 30 findings: Error: page.evaluate: TypeError: Cannot convert undefined or null to object'. The loop reaches tokenFit, which needs the tokens as a second argument (Object.entries(tokens) on undefined). The README says one line later that tokenFit takes a second argument, but the loop it prints passes none, so the example cannot run to its end and the four lines after it (grade, repairPlan, receiptText) are never reached. (Separately: under tsx the function text carries a helper call `__name` and the loop fails at once with 'ReferenceError: __name is not defined'; the script below defines it first so that the README's own fault shows. Vitest adds no such call.)

input: blindScore with 60 answers on each kind of page from 6 reviewers, none judged person-made (line H1 of tru-logic.mts), and with every answer judged person-made on both kinds. Compared with packages/kit/src/logic/blindTest.ts: "\"Indistinguishable\" is never proven; the most a test can say is that it found no difference and how large a difference it could have missed." and blind-test/PROTOCOL.md: "It can show that the test **found no difference**, and how large a difference it could have missed. It can never prove that the two kinds are the same."
observed: Line H1: 'Reviewers judged 0% of the tool-built pages and 0% of the person-made pages to be made by a person. The test found no clear difference; the true difference could be as large as 0%. The range treats every answer as independent, so it is too narrow when few reviewers give many answers.' With the protocol's own minimum met (5 reviewers, 30 answers each), the statement says the largest difference the test could have missed is 0%, which is the claim that the two kinds are the same. Cause: the range of the difference uses the simple formula Z*sqrt(p(1-p)/n), which is zero when a share is 0% or 100%, while shareOf uses the Wilson interval (for 0 of 60 it gives a high end of about 6%). Line H3: shareOf(5, 3) returns share 1.67 with low and high null (no check that the count fits).

input: Does the good page pass because the checks are sound or because it avoids hard cases? Ran all 28 checks on packages/kit/fixtures/good.html at 1280 and 320 and read which rules answer 'not-applicable'; then removed planted defects one at a time (a script deleted, for each of the 36 page-check records, the line of flawed.html marked data-defect="<rule id>" and reran that rule's check).

So every rule is exercised on the good page at one of the two widths; none passes by being not-applicable at both. Removal run: for 33 of 36 records the rule stopped failing when its marked line was removed; the three exceptions are neuro-reflow, fit-radii, fit-unused-color (attempts TRU-4 and TRU-5). The good page does avoid hard cases (attempts TRU-13 to TRU-17 are one-line changes to it that a careful person would call faulty and that still grade "Crafted"), which PROGRESS.md concedes in general terms ("each was tried on one planted defect"). No separate finding here.
